title: Spec: JS↔WASM ABI conventions for perf kernels
description:
# Goal
Define a **single, consistent** JS↔WASM ABI pattern that we will reuse across new kernels (k-mer counting, dotplot, diff, PCA).

## Background / current pain
We already have wasm-compute functions that return JSON strings or require object-heavy conversions. That’s fine for one-off calls, but it leaves performance on the table and increases GC pressure.

The biggest risk in WASM work is not the Rust kernel—it’s the boundary:
- Sending huge strings repeatedly
- Returning JSON blobs that must be parsed
- Unclear ownership (`free()` vs GC) and memory leaks
- Inconsistent handling of ambiguous bases and determinism

## Proposed ABI standards
### Inputs
- Prefer **Uint8Array** for sequences (ASCII bytes or encoded 0-4 codes) when the caller already has bytes.
- Provide **string convenience wrappers** only when it’s measurably acceptable.
- Avoid per-call allocations when possible (allow passing preallocated output buffers or return typed arrays).

### Outputs
- Prefer **typed arrays** (Uint32Array / Float32Array / Uint8Array) ready for rendering.
- Avoid JSON in hot paths.
- When multiple arrays are returned, define a compact struct layout (header + flat arrays) or multiple typed arrays.

### Ownership & lifetime
- wasm-bindgen objects must document whether `.free()` is required.
- For raw typed arrays returned from WASM (`Vec<T>`), define whether JS receives a copied array or a view.

### Determinism
- No `Math.random()` equivalent in the algorithm core.
- Define how we handle sign ambiguity for PCA eigenvectors.

### Ambiguous bases
- Define and document: any base outside A/C/G/T resets rolling k-mer state.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Documented conventions are agreed-on and referenced by subsequent WASM beads.
- [ ] At least one concrete example ABI is specified for: (1) k-mer counts, (2) MinHash signature, (3) dotplot buffer.
- [ ] The conventions explicitly address: typed-array I/O, ownership, determinism, ambiguous bases.
close_reason: Created comprehensive WASM_ABI_SPEC.md documenting: (1) bytes-first input conventions, (2) typed-array output patterns, (3) ownership/.free() rules, (4) determinism guarantees, (5) ambiguous base handling, and (6) concrete example ABIs for k-mer counts, MinHash signatures, and dotplot buffers. Unblocks 10 dependent beads.

title: Infra: worker-safe wasm-compute loader (cached init + error surface)
description:
# Goal
Create a single, reusable WASM loader pattern that works in:
- Main thread (React components)
- Module workers (Vite `?worker` bundles)

## Why
We currently have multiple ad-hoc patterns (some in workers, some in utils). For more WASM adoption, we need:
- One-time initialization
- Cached module instance
- Clear error messages and fallback behavior

## Requirements
- Must be safe to call concurrently (multiple callers awaiting the same promise).
- Must work in workers without relying on Node globals.
- Must allow optional feature detection (SIMD, threads if ever used).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] One exported helper that returns an initialized wasm-compute module.
- [ ] Works in both main thread and workers.
- [ ] Has deterministic fallback behavior if wasm import fails.
- [ ] Logs are dev-only and structured (no spam).
close_reason: Created centralized wasm-loader.ts with cached init, concurrent caller deduplication, worker-safe design, and dev-only logging. Updated structure.worker.ts to use new loader as adoption example. Unblocks 12 dependent beads.

title: Workers: pass genome sequences as bytes (SharedArrayBuffer / ArrayBuffer)
description:
# Goal
Stop repeatedly cloning giant genome strings between main thread and workers.

## Current state
`ComputeOrchestrator` and `SharedSequencePool` already exist, but `analysis.worker.ts` still receives sequences as strings (see TODOs in `ComputeOrchestrator.ts`).

## Plan
- Define a worker request shape that can carry:
  - `SharedArrayBuffer` (best) or transferable `ArrayBuffer`
  - length
  - optional encoding (ASCII vs 0-4 codes)
- Update orchestrator + worker APIs to accept the byte form.

## Why this matters
Even if compute is in WASM, paying the cost of (string clone → uppercase → replace → slice) per analysis is slow and GC-heavy.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A worker API can accept a byte-backed sequence reference.
- [ ] When SharedArrayBuffer is available, no copy of the underlying sequence occurs.
- [ ] When not available, transferable ArrayBuffer is used instead of structured-cloned strings where feasible.
close_reason: Complete: All acceptance criteria met - analysis.worker.runAnalysisShared accepts byte-backed SequenceBytesRef, SharedSequencePool handles SAB zero-copy when available, ArrayBuffer transfer fallback when not. Subtasks 8qk2.3.1 and 8qk2.3.2 already closed.

title: Define byte-backed request/response types (Comlink + Transferable)
description:
# Goal
Define the *canonical* byte-backed sequence request/response types used between the main thread and module workers.

This bead is intentionally “boring plumbing”: we want one stable shape so every new WASM kernel can plug in without re-inventing transport.

# Background
Today some worker APIs still accept genome sequences as JS strings. For larger genomes this creates avoidable costs:
- structured-clone of a long string
- repeated `toUpperCase()` / regex cleanup / slicing
- GC churn from temporary strings

As we move more kernels to Rust/WASM, we want workers to consume **bytes-first** (typed arrays) so the hot loops don’t pay JS string overhead.

# Scope (what this bead defines)
## Sequence encoding contract
Pick a small set of encodings and document them explicitly:
- `ascii` — raw ASCII bytes (A/C/G/T/N plus lower-case variants)
- `acgt05` — encoded bases (A=0, C=1, G=2, T=3, N/other=4) as `Uint8Array`

Notes:
- `ascii` is convenient because we can generate it once from DB strings and reuse.
- `acgt05` is what many WASM kernels want internally. We can either encode on the JS side once (and cache) or encode inside WASM.

## Transport reference (SAB vs AB)
Define a `SequenceBytesRef` union that supports:
- `SharedArrayBuffer` when `crossOriginIsolated === true`
- transferable `ArrayBuffer` fallback when SAB is unavailable

Example shape (names may vary):
- `kind: 'sab' | 'ab'`
- `buffer: SharedArrayBuffer | ArrayBuffer`
- `byteOffset`, `byteLength`
- `encoding`
- optional `sequenceId` / `version` for caching keys

## Worker request/response shapes
Define request/response types for:
- analysis.worker
- dotplot.worker
- comparison.worker

Guidelines:
- Inputs should be small objects + typed arrays.
- Outputs should prefer typed arrays and use Transferables for big buffers.
- Avoid JSON for hot paths.

# Browser compatibility / constraints
- SAB requires COOP/COEP (cross-origin isolation). Many embedded contexts and older browsers won’t have it.
- Transferables (`postMessage(..., [arrayBuffer])`) are widely supported and should be the default fallback.
- Keep types usable in both Comlink-wrapped and plain postMessage workers.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] TypeScript types exist for byte-backed sequences (SAB + transferable AB) and are imported by `ComputeOrchestrator` and at least one worker.
- [ ] The encoding contract is written down in the type docs (what values mean, how invalid bases behave).
- [ ] The shapes are designed so callers can supply a transfer list without awkward wrapping.
close_reason: Added canonical byte-backed sequence/worker message types (SequenceEncoding/SequenceBytesRef) and updated SharedSequenceRef + ComputeOrchestrator + dotplot/comparison workers to use them.

title: ComputeOrchestrator: plumb SharedSequencePool bytes into analysis requests
description:
# Goal
Plumb the new byte-backed sequence transport through `ComputeOrchestrator` so workers can analyze genomes without cloning giant strings.

This bead is the “wiring” step that makes `phage_explorer-8qk2.3.1` real.

# Background
We already have `SharedSequencePool` and orchestration code, but some analyses still end up shipping sequences as strings to workers. That’s a performance cliff:
- copying/serializing huge strings
- repeated normalization work (uppercase, replace ambiguous chars)
- poor cache reuse across multiple overlays

# Plan
## 1) Source of truth: SharedSequencePool
- Ensure the pool can provide a `SequenceBytesRef` (SAB when possible, transferable AB otherwise).
- Ensure it can return a stable `sequenceId`/`version` key for caching (e.g., based on phage id + genome hash).

## 2) Orchestrator request construction
Update the orchestration layer so *every* worker request that needs the full genome can accept bytes:
- analysis.worker (GC skew, k-mer spectra, repeats, etc.)
- dotplot.worker
- comparison.worker

Guidelines:
- Prefer passing `{ sequenceRef }` not `{ sequenceString }`.
- When using transferable AB, include it in the transfer list to avoid a copy.

## 3) Progressive enhancement
- If `crossOriginIsolated` and SAB path is enabled, prefer SAB for zero-copy.
- Else, fall back to transferable AB.
- As a last resort, keep string path in orchestrator for truly unsupported edge cases.

# Risks / gotchas
- Transferable AB is one-shot: once transferred, the sender’s view is detached. The pool must own the buffer (or copy once into a pool-owned buffer).
- SAB requires COOP/COEP; we can’t assume it everywhere.
- Avoid “double encoding” where we convert DB string → ASCII bytes → encoded codes multiple times.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] At least one real analysis request uses byte-backed sequences end-to-end (main → worker) without string cloning.
- [ ] When SAB is available, orchestrator uses it (verify via logging/dev instrumentation).
- [ ] When SAB is not available, orchestrator uses a transferable AB path (verify the buffer is transferred, not cloned).
- [ ] String path remains as compatibility fallback.
close_reason: Wired byte-backed sequence refs into dotplot/comparison postMessage + analysis.worker shared API (SAB/transferable AB), keeping string fallbacks

title: analysis.worker: byte→uppercased-base decoding helpers (no huge intermediate strings)
description:
# Goal
Add small, reusable utilities in `analysis.worker.ts` for operating on **byte-backed sequences** efficiently.

This bead is the worker-side counterpart to the orchestrator work in `phage_explorer-8qk2.3.*`.

# Background
Once the worker receives bytes, we need to avoid immediately converting them back into a giant JS string (which would recreate the exact GC/memory problem we’re trying to solve).

We want a handful of primitives that make the common patterns cheap:
- “is this base A/C/G/T?”
- “normalize to uppercase/known alphabet”
- “rolling 2-bit k-mer index update”

# Design notes
## Prefer small helpers over giant abstractions
The worker already has a lot going on. The goal is:
- keep helpers tiny and inlinable
- avoid per-window allocations

## Recommended representations
Support the encodings defined in `phage_explorer-8qk2.3.1`:
- `ascii` bytes: read-only, convenient to ship
- `acgt05` codes: ideal for WASM kernels and tight loops

## Helper candidates
- `isACGTAsciiByte(b: number): boolean`
- `asciiToAcgt05(b: number): 0|1|2|3|4`
- `encodeAsciiToAcgt05(src: Uint8Array, dst?: Uint8Array): Uint8Array`
- `rolling2bitUpdate(state, code, k)` (with N/invalid reset semantics)

Important: ambiguous bases MUST be handled deterministically and documented:
- anything not A/C/G/T → reset rolling state (no k-mer emitted spanning ambiguity)

# Browser considerations
- Avoid `TextDecoder` + giant string unless absolutely needed.
- Typed-array loops should be written so they don’t accidentally allocate (`map`, `slice`, `concat`).

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] analysis.worker can run at least one existing analysis *entirely* on bytes without converting to a string.
- [ ] Helpers match the ABI rules for ambiguous bases (N resets).
- [ ] Helpers are used by at least one WASM-wired kernel integration bead (k-mer/dotplot/diff).
close_reason: Added bytes-native helpers (ascii→acgt05 + rolling2bit with ambiguity reset) and implemented gc-skew directly on SequenceBytesRef without decoding huge strings; fixed dense-kmer import path

title: WASM: SequenceHandle prototype (store encoded DNA in WASM memory)
description:
# Goal
Prototype a `SequenceHandle` concept in wasm-compute that stores an encoded genome once and exposes fast methods.

## Why
Many overlays run multiple analyses over the same genome. Even if each analysis is in WASM, re-copying the entire sequence each call can erase wins.

## Design sketch
- `SequenceHandle::new(seq_bytes)` stores an encoded representation in WASM memory.
- Exposes methods like:
  - `count_kmers(k)`
  - `minhash(num_hashes, k)`
  - `gc_skew(window, step)`

## Constraints
- Must keep memory bounded (LRU or explicit free on phage change).
- Must not bloat wasm bundle or complicate build.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A minimal handle exists and can compute at least one kernel without re-copying the whole sequence.
- [ ] Clear lifetime rules and `.free()` semantics.
close_reason:
SequenceHandle prototype complete:

**Implementation:**
- `SequenceHandle` struct stores encoded DNA in WASM memory
- Encoding: A=0, C=1, G=2, T=3, N=4 (case-insensitive)
- Constructor encodes once, methods reuse without re-copying

**Methods implemented:**
- `gc_skew(window, step)` - sliding window GC skew values
- `cumulative_gc_skew()` - running G-C sum for ori/ter detection
- `count_kmers(k)` - dense k-mer counting (k ≤ 10)
- `minhash(num_hashes, k)` - canonical MinHash signature

**Memory management:**
- `.free()` releases WASM memory (wasm-bindgen default)
- Clear lifetime rules documented

**Test coverage:**
- 8 new unit tests (encoding, N handling, gc_skew, kmers, minhash)
- All 26 WASM tests pass

**TypeScript types:**
- Full type definitions in index.d.ts with usage examples

Unblocks phage_explorer-8qk2.6 (adopt in hot kernels).

title: Compat: browser feature matrix + progressive enhancement (WASM/SAB/SIMD)
description:
# Goal
Ensure new performance features (WASM kernels, zero-copy sequences) work across a wide browser set **without** slowing down modern browsers.

This bead is about *progressive enhancement*: pick the best available path at runtime and keep a safe fallback.

# Background
Our perf roadmap increasingly relies on platform features with uneven support:
- `SharedArrayBuffer` (requires COOP/COEP / crossOriginIsolated)
- module workers bundling behavior differences (Safari vs Chromium)
- WASM feature flags (SIMD now common but not universal)

If we don’t design this explicitly, we’ll accidentally:
- break older browsers
- regress modern browsers by always using lowest-common-denominator paths

# What this bead delivers
## 1) Browser feature matrix (documented)
Define the minimum supported set and how features map to behavior:
- WebAssembly baseline
- WASM SIMD (optional fast path)
- SharedArrayBuffer / crossOriginIsolated (zero-copy)
- Transferable ArrayBuffer fallback

Include at least:
- Chrome (desktop + Android)
- Firefox (desktop)
- Safari (desktop + iOS)

## 2) Centralized runtime feature detection
Create a single place that answers questions like:
- `canUseWasm()`
- `canUseWasmSimd()` (if we build a SIMD variant)
- `canUseSharedArrayBuffer()`

Guidelines:
- No UA sniffing; feature-detect.
- Keep it side-effect free.

## 3) Policy decisions captured in code
Examples:
- If SAB unavailable: use transferable AB.
- If WASM import fails: fall back to JS kernels.
- Never block the UI while probing features.

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] There is a documented matrix for what happens on each browser tier.
- [ ] Feature detection is centralized and reused by workers/orchestrator.
- [ ] Every new WASM bead references this policy (so we don’t fork behavior ad-hoc).
close_reason: Implemented browser-capabilities.ts with centralized feature detection (canUseWasm, canUseWasmSimd, canUseSharedArrayBuffer), browser support matrix documentation, and progressive enhancement policies. Updated utils/wasm.ts to re-export from centralized module.

title: (Optional) WASM: multi-variant build (baseline + SIMD) + runtime selection
description:
# Goal
Explore building a SIMD-enabled wasm-compute variant for modern browsers while keeping a baseline build for maximum compatibility.

# Why
Some kernels (dotplot, PCA, k-mer vector math) can benefit significantly from SIMD on supported engines.

But we must not:
- break older browsers
- slow down modern browsers via expensive probing

# Strategy sketch
- Produce two wasm artifacts:
  - baseline (no SIMD)
  - simd-enabled
- At runtime:
  - detect SIMD support (or attempt instantiation) quickly
  - load SIMD module when supported
  - fall back to baseline otherwise

# Constraints
- Keep bundle size under control (avoid doubling always-downloaded bytes).
- Prefer lazy loading in workers only.
- Ensure the loader caches the chosen variant (no repeated probing).

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] SIMD variant is used on a SIMD-capable browser and measurable speedups are observed.
- [ ] Baseline variant loads everywhere else.
- [ ] No regressions in cold-start time on common devices.
close_reason: Implemented baseline+SIMD wasm-compute build + runtime selection

title: Add React.memo() to expensive components - prevent unnecessary re-renders

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
## Add React.memo() to Expensive Components

### Problem
None of the major visualization components use React.memo():
- Model3DView (1106 lines) - complex 3D rendering
- SequenceView (806 lines) - canvas-based sequence display
- GeneMapCanvas (300+ lines) - gene annotation visualization

Without memo, these components re-render whenever ANY parent state changes, even if their own props haven't changed. This is especially wasteful for:
- Theme changes in unrelated components
- Zustand store updates for unrelated state slices
- Parent layout adjustments

### Solution

#### 1. Wrap components with memo():
```typescript
// Before
export function Model3DView(props: Props) { ... }

// After  
export const Model3DView = memo(function Model3DView(props: Props) {
  // ...existing implementation
});
```

#### 2. Add useMemo() for expensive derived values:
```typescript
// Camera object created once, not every render
const camera = useMemo(() => new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(...), [fov]);

// Theme colors computed once per theme change
const colors = useMemo(() => computeThemeColors(theme), [theme.id]);
```

#### 3. Add useCallback() for event handlers passed as props:
```typescript
const handleClick = useCallback((e) => { ... }, [dependencies]);
```

### Files to Modify
1. `packages/web/src/components/Model3DView.tsx`
2. `packages/web/src/components/SequenceView.tsx`
3. `packages/web/src/components/GeneMapCanvas.tsx`

### Key Areas in Each:
- Model3DView: camera, controls, lighting setup objects
- SequenceView: grid building, color computations
- GeneMapCanvas: gene position calculations, canvas context

### Impact
- 50%+ reduction in unnecessary re-renders
- Smoother UI during state changes
- Lower CPU usage during interactions

### Testing
1. Open React DevTools Profiler
2. Navigate between phages, toggle overlays, change themes
3. Verify memoized components don't re-render when their props unchanged
4. Before/after flame graph comparison

notes:
## COCKTAIL RESISTANCE EVOLUTION SIMULATOR

**Full Implementation from Roadmap**

### Concept
Simulate resistance emergence under single vs cocktail regimens using genome-derived parameters (receptor diversity, anti-defense, spacer proximity).

### How to Build

**Stochastic Engine:**
- Gillespie/tau-leaping in Rust+WASM (rand + rayon)
- Events: bacterial growth, phage adsorption, resistance mutation, receptor switching

**Genome-Derived Parameters:**
- Receptor diversity from tail fiber annotation
- Sie genes (superinfection exclusion)
- CRISPR spacer matches (immunity potential)
- Anti-defense gene count

**User Inputs:**
- MOI (multiplicity of infection)
- Dosing cadence (hours between doses)
- Population size (CFU/mL)
- Cocktail composition (1-5 phages)

**Outputs:**
- Probability of resistance over time
- Time-to-resistance distribution
- Compare mono vs cocktail curves
- Optimal cocktail selection

### TUI Features
- Live ASCII trajectories (multiple runs overlaid)
- Risk meter updates in real-time
- Side-by-side mono vs cocktail comparison
- Sliders: MOI, dose interval, population size
- Toggle 'optimize cocktail' to auto-pick best trio
- Resistance probability timeline
- [R]un new simulation, [C]ompare, [O]ptimize

### Why It's Good
- Turns genomic evidence into therapy guidance
- Quantifies resistance risk over time
- Compares mono vs cocktail robustness

description:
## Animated, Interactive Biological Visualizations

### Philosophy
These aren't just illustrations—they're interactive tools that make abstract biology tangible. The goal is to create 'aha moments' where complex concepts suddenly click.

### Visual 1: DNA Helix Explorer
**What it shows:**
- 3D double helix you can rotate/zoom
- Click nucleotides to see base pairing
- Follow the backbone (sugar-phosphate)
- See major/minor grooves
- Animate unwinding for replication

**Technical approach:**
- Three.js for 3D rendering
- Simplified model (10-20 base pairs)
- Annotations on hover
- 'DNA basics' link to module

### Visual 2: Translation Visualizer
**What it shows:**
- mRNA strand moving through ribosome
- tRNAs delivering amino acids
- Codon-anticodon matching
- Growing polypeptide chain
- Stop codon and release

**Technical approach:**
- Canvas 2D animation
- Step-by-step or continuous mode
- Current codon highlighted
- Speed control

### Visual 3: Codon Wheel/Table
**What it shows:**
- All 64 codons organized by first/second/third position
- Color by amino acid property (hydrophobic, polar, charged)
- Click codon → show amino acid info
- Search by amino acid → highlight codons

**Technical approach:**
- SVG or Canvas
- Two views: wheel and table
- Filter by property

### Visual 4: Phage Infection Animation
**What it shows:**
- Phage attaching to bacterial surface
- DNA injection (tail contraction)
- Replication inside host
- Assembly of new phages
- Lysis and release

**Technical approach:**
- Canvas 2D or CSS animation
- Timeline control (scrub through stages)
- Stage annotations
- Option for lytic vs lysogenic path

### Visual 5: Reading Frame Demo
**What it shows:**
- Same DNA sequence in all 3 forward frames
- Visual shift showing different amino acids
- Stop codon positions highlighted
- Why frame matters for ORF finding

**Technical approach:**
- Interactive sequence display
- Frame selector (1, 2, 3)
- Real-time translation update

### Files to Create
- packages/web/src/education/visualizers/DNAHelixViz.tsx
- packages/web/src/education/visualizers/TranslationViz.tsx
- packages/web/src/education/visualizers/CodonWheelViz.tsx
- packages/web/src/education/visualizers/InfectionViz.tsx
- packages/web/src/education/visualizers/ReadingFrameViz.tsx

### Integration
- Embedded in foundational modules
- Standalone access from 'Explore' menu
- Context panels can show relevant visualizer

### Why Prioritize Visuals
Biology textbooks are full of static diagrams. Interactive visualizations are what make concepts truly click. These create the 'beautiful' reaction that drives engagement and learning.

title: EPIC: Remove or reach the unreachable — dead overlays, dead exports, dead utilities
description:
## Origin

The 2026-09-01 reality check traced reachability for every overlay id, every Rust export,
and several utility modules. A substantial amount of the codebase cannot be reached by a
user at all, while continuing to appear in type unions, menus, and documentation.

## Why this is worth an epic rather than piecemeal cleanup

AGENTS.md is explicit: "We optimize for a clean architecture now, not backwards
compatibility. No compat shims or v2 file clones. When changing behavior, migrate callers
and remove old code inside the same file. The bar for adding files is very high."

Dead code in this repository is not inert. It is actively misleading, because agents and
humans read it as specification: `featureRegistry.ts` documents 18 wrong shortcuts,
`collaboration` implies a session-sharing feature that BroadcastChannel cannot provide,
and 24 dead Rust exports make the WASM layer look far more integrated than it is. Every
one of these has already misled someone — several are the direct cause of README claims
that turned out to be false.

## Hard constraint

AGENTS.md RULE 1 forbids deleting any file without explicit written approval in-session.
Every child bead that proposes deletion must therefore end by *asking*, with the specific
list of files, and must not run a deletion command until approval is given and recorded.
Where deletion is blocked, the fallback is to make the dead thing reachable or to mark it
clearly.

## Definition of done

Each child reaches a recorded decision — wire it up, or get approval and remove it — with
no item left in the ambiguous middle.

title: The tour overlay id has no component and FeatureTour is never mounted
description:
## Findings

`tour` is a member of the `OverlayId` union
(`packages/web/src/components/overlays/OverlayProvider.tsx:66-124`) but has no case in
`OverlayManager.tsx` — it is the only id of 58 with no render path.

`packages/web/src/components/overlays/FeatureTour.tsx` exists and is exported from
`packages/web/src/components/overlays/index.ts:28`, but no file imports it, and nothing
calls `open('tour')`.

## Context

The Zustand store persists tour completion state (README, State Management: "LocalStorage
persistence: Beginner mode, tour completion, theme preference"), and the store tracks
"completed tours" among its user-domain properties. So there is state machinery for a
feature the user can never start.

The onboarding story around it does work: WelcomeModal and KeyboardPrimer are mounted and
shown on first run. The tour is the missing third piece.

## The fix

Either mount FeatureTour and give it an entry point (a "Take the tour" action in the
welcome modal and the Command Palette is the obvious placement), or seek approval to remove
the component, the union member, and the associated store state together.

Mounting is preferable: the README markets progressive disclosure for newcomers, and a
guided tour is the strongest version of that promise.

## Acceptance criteria

- `tour` either opens something or no longer exists in the union.
- No orphaned store state remains for a removed feature.

title: Collaboration overlay is unreachable and its transport cannot do what its UI promises
description:
## Findings

Two separate problems.

**Unreachable.** `collaboration` is lazy-registered
(`packages/web/src/components/overlays/OverlayManager.tsx:57`, case at `:355`) but
nothing anywhere calls `open('collaboration')` — not App.tsx, not the ActionRegistry, not
featureRegistry, not share-state. No user can open it.

**Cannot work as presented.** `packages/web/src/collaboration/CollaborationManager.ts:4-5`
states plainly: "Manages local peer state synchronization via BroadcastChannel. Simulates a
collaborative session across tabs". `:60,:72` open
`new BroadcastChannel('phage_explorer_collab')`. BroadcastChannel is same-origin,
same-browser only. The overlay's UI nonetheless offers name / session / chat inputs and
Create / Join / Copy / Leave buttons — a join-by-session-id flow that cannot cross machines.

`packages/web/src/collaboration/types.ts:35-40` declares
`SignalingMessage { offer | answer | candidate }` — WebRTC vocabulary that is never used.
There are zero occurrences of `RTCPeerConnection` or `RTCDataChannel` in the repository,
and no signaling endpoint exists (no `api/` functions in vercel.json;
`packages/web/src/api/` holds only NCBI, Serratus and SRA clients).

## Tracker history

The originating bead `8kpa` ("[WEB-P5] Collaborative Sessions: WebRTC Real-Time") and its
six children were all closed on 2025-12-08 with no close reason and no comments, as part of
a 221-bead mass closure. A later bead (`zati`, 2025-12-17) honestly re-scoped the feature
to BroadcastChannel, but the original never reopened and the UI was never re-scoped with it.

## The fix, in order of increasing ambition

1. **Honest scope now:** rename to something true ("Sync across tabs"), make it reachable,
   and remove the join-by-id affordance that implies remote peers.
2. **Or park it:** seek approval to remove the overlay, the manager, and the unused
   signaling types.
3. **Or build it:** implement real WebRTC with a signaling endpoint. This is a genuinely
   large piece of work and should be its own epic if chosen — do not let the current stub
   stand in for it.

## Acceptance criteria

- No UI offers a capability the transport cannot deliver.
- A decision among the three options is recorded here.
- If the feature stays, it is reachable from the Command Palette.

title: Selection pressure dN/dS engine is real but dead in the browser
description:
## Findings

`packages/core/src/selection-pressure.ts:22-224` implements a genuine dN/dS estimator, and
recent work (`2bae16f`) made it gene-aware with reverse-frame correctness. It is one of the
better pieces of analysis in the repository.

In the web app it never runs. It requires `diffReferenceSequence`, and `setDiffReference`
is called only by the TUI (`packages/tui/src/components/App.tsx:538`). In the browser the
overlay always renders its empty state.

Compounding this, the overlay is nearly unreachable anyway: `selectionPressure` has no
entry in `packages/web/src/keyboard/actionRegistry.ts`, so it appears in neither the
Analysis Menu (built from the registry, `AnalysisMenu.tsx:177-180`) nor the Command
Palette (`CommandPalette.tsx:465`). Its only openers are
`packages/web/src/components/mobile/SelectedGeneDock.tsx:493` and the dead
`lib/featureRegistry.ts:587` — i.e. it is mobile-only by accident.

## Why it matters

The README lists "Selection Pressure Chromosome Painter (dN/dS Landscape)" among the
project's analyses, and the CHANGELOG advertises the gene-aware reverse-frame work. A user
on desktop cannot reach it, and a user on mobile who reaches it sees nothing.

## The fix

- Set the diff reference in the web app when a comparison target is chosen. The comparison
  overlay already selects a second phage; wire that selection into `setDiffReference`.
- Add an ActionRegistry entry so the overlay is reachable from the menu and palette on
  every surface.
- Ensure the empty state explains what the user must do ("select a comparison phage")
  rather than appearing broken.

## Acceptance criteria

- Selecting a comparison phage populates the dN/dS landscape in the web app.
- The overlay is listed in the Analysis Menu and Command Palette.
- An e2e test opens it after selecting a reference and asserts non-empty output.
close_reason: Fixed at 5278d87. Two independent gaps, both closed. (1) Nothing loaded the reference genome in the browser: toggleDiff sets diffReferencePhageId but not the sequence, and only the TUI had a loader. Added useDiffReferenceSequence, mounted once at app level so diff rendering in the sequence grid benefits too. (2) The overlay had no ActionRegistry entry, so it was absent from the Analysis Menu and Command Palette and reachable only from the mobile gene dock; registered under Analysis on Alt+Shift+S. The empty state also gave one message for three situations and now distinguishes diff-off, reference-loading and analysis-running. Verified by packages/web/src/hooks/useDiffReferenceSequence.test.ts (6 tests) covering the store contract and registry wiring, including a discrimination check so the shortcut-conflict assertion cannot pass vacuously.

title: GPU/WASM benchmark overlay is listed in menus but renders nothing in production
description:
## Findings

`gpuWasmBenchmark` is registered with `surfaces: ['web']` in
`packages/web/src/keyboard/actionRegistry.ts:830-840`, so it appears in the Analysis Menu
and Command Palette in production. The component returns `null` unless running in DEV
(`packages/web/src/components/overlays/GpuWasmBenchmarkOverlay.tsx:551`).

A production user can find it, select it, and get nothing — with no explanation.

## The fix

Either gate the registry entry on DEV so it does not appear in production, or ship the
overlay for real. The second option is attractive: this overlay is the only place in the
repository that measures WASM against JS, and the WASM epic needs exactly that capability
to substantiate or retire the README's speedup claims. If it ships, note the gaps found in
the audit — it has a JS baseline only for dense-kmer, none for minhash or gc-skew, and it
computes no speedup ratio.

## Acceptance criteria

- The menu entry appears only where the overlay renders.
- If shipped, it reports a JS-vs-WASM ratio for every operation it lists.

title: offline.html and the File System Access utilities are built but never used
description:
## Findings

**offline.html** — `packages/web/public/offline.html` exists and is precached, but no code
in `packages/web/src` references it. It was the deliverable of bead `nmi` ("Create
offline.html fallback page"), closed 2025-12-07. The service worker does have a
NavigationRoute app-shell fallback (`packages/web/src/sw.ts:219`), so offline navigation
works — via index.html, not this page. Lighthouse CI runs audits against it as a second URL,
which is currently the only thing that loads it.

**File System Access** — `packages/web/src/utils/fileSystem.ts:33-34,64-65` wraps
`showSaveFilePicker` and `showOpenFilePicker`; `packages/web/src/hooks/useFileSystem.ts:3`
wraps that; and the only consumer is the barrel re-export at `hooks/index.ts:18`. No
component calls it. It was bead `xree` ("Add File System Access API integration"), closed
2025-12-08 with no reason.

The deploy plan (PLAN_TO_DEPLOY, "Novel Web Capabilities") lists the File System Access API
as one of six browser-only capabilities that justify the web app's existence.

## The fix

**offline.html:** either wire the service worker to serve it for navigation failures, or
seek approval to remove it (and drop it from the Lighthouse URL list).

**File System Access:** wire it to a real user need — exporting analysis results, saving a
dot plot or CGR image, importing a custom FASTA — or seek approval to remove it. Export is
the obvious fit: several overlays produce data a researcher would want to keep, and the
sequence-logo overlay already accepts a pasted custom alignment, so import has a precedent.

Note that the viewer sandbox does not restrict this app (it is a normal web page), so the
API works where the browser supports it.

## Acceptance criteria

- Each item is either reachable by a user or removed with recorded approval.

title: HGT overlay passes an empty reference library so the donor panel can never render
description:
## Findings

`packages/web/src/components/overlays/HGTOverlay.tsx:321` passes `{}` as the reference
library to `analyzeHGTProvenance`. With no references, the donor-lineage panel the overlay
advertises has nothing to compute and cannot render.

This compounds a second defect in the same path: `packages/comparison/src/hgt-tracer.ts`
wires MinHash signature acceleration at `:43-45` but its initializer is never called
(`:60-61`, "REMOVED to prevent side effects/crashes"), so `precomputeReferenceSignatures`
returns null (`:408`) and the code falls back to exact k=15 Set Jaccard (`:467-475`) —
which would matter a great deal if references were actually supplied.

## Context

The README describes "Recombination Radar — k-mer Jaccard similarity against reference
panel; detects mosaic segments & HGT breakpoints" and, under Alignment-Free Genomics,
"Plot 'donor' assignment along the genome … direct evidence of recombination events".
NEW_IDEAS Top-10 idea 7 ("HGT Provenance Tracer") specifies a passport-stamp UI with an
island bar and a donor pie chart.

## The fix

Supply a real reference panel. The 24 catalog genomes are the natural first panel — every
other phage in the database is a candidate donor, and their sequences are already local.
Precompute sketches at build time into phage.db so the overlay does not have to load 23
genomes at runtime (an existing closed bead proposed exactly this sketch table; it was
never built).

Then re-enable the WASM MinHash path once the initialization defect in the WASM epic is
fixed, since a 24-way comparison is precisely the workload it was written for.

## Acceptance criteria

- The donor panel renders with real donor candidates for a phage with mosaic structure.
- A test asserts a non-empty reference panel reaches the analyzer.
close_reason: Fixed at 60a1054. Extracted the TUI's inline reference-panel loader into packages/comparison/src/reference-panel.ts and wired the web overlay to it; the catalogue is the donor panel, excluding the phage under analysis. Verified by packages/comparison/src/reference-panel.test.ts (12 tests) which asserts the capability rather than the plumbing: with an empty panel the analyzer detects islands but names no donor; with the panel supplied it names one, and that donor is the reference whose composition matches the island. Also covers exclusion, both caps, abort, and the unreadable-reference path. The overlay now states how many references it is comparing against, so an empty Putative Donors section no longer reads as 'no transfer detected'.

title: Twenty-four Rust exports and every SequenceHandle accessor are dead code
description:
## Findings

The Rust crate exports far more than the TypeScript ever calls. Exports with zero
TypeScript references outside `pkg/` and the `.d.ts` files:

`translate_sequence`, `reverse_complement`, `calculate_gc_content`,
`is_valid_dense_kmer_k`, `get_dense_kmer_max_k`, `pca_power_iteration` (the f64
variant; only f32 is used), `hoeffdings_d`, `kmer_hoeffdings_d`, `shannon_entropy`,
`shannon_entropy_from_counts`, `jensen_shannon_divergence`,
`jensen_shannon_divergence_from_counts`, `compute_linguistic_complexity`,
`compute_windowed_complexity`, `build_grid`, `encode_sequence_fast`,
`compute_micro_runs`, `compute_diff_mask`, `compute_diff_mask_encoded`,
`kl_divergence_dense`, `parse_pdb`, and the whole `renderer.rs` surface
(`render_ascii_model`, `Model3D`, `Vector3` — `packages/renderer-3d` uses its own
TypeScript `Model3D` interface at `packages/renderer-3d/src/models.ts:7`).

Additionally every `SequenceHandle` accessor except `dotplot_self` is unused:
`length`, `valid_count`, `gc_skew`, `cumulative_gc_skew`, `count_kmers`, `minhash`,
`encoded_bytes`.

Separately, five exports are *wired* but unreachable because their initializers are never
called: `analyze_kmers`, `min_hash_jaccard`, `minhash_signature`,
`minhash_signature_canonical`, `minhash_jaccard_from_signatures` — see the WASM epic.

## Why it matters

Three concrete costs:

1. It is why the README's WASM table is wrong — `translate_sequence` and
   `reverse_complement` exist, so the claim looks true from the Rust side.
2. Every dead export is compiled into both shipped WASM variants, which are base64-inlined
   into the bundle (~238 kB + ~288 kB of asset payload).
3. `parse_pdb` in particular is a trap: the web app has its own TypeScript PDB parser
   (`structure-loader.ts:243`), so a reader will reasonably assume the Rust one is the one
   in use.

## The fix

For each export, choose deliberately: wire it (several are genuinely better than their JS
counterparts — `SequenceHandle` exists precisely to avoid re-encoding the sequence for
each kernel, which is the zero-copy story `docs/wasm-abi.md` describes), or seek approval
to remove it.

Note the interaction with the bytes-first ABI bead: adopting `SequenceHandle` for GC skew,
entropy, codon counting and repeat detection would simultaneously kill most of this dead
code and deliver the zero-copy behavior the ABI spec requires.

## Acceptance criteria

- Every listed export is wired, or removed with recorded approval.
- The shipped WASM shrinks measurably if exports are removed.

title: Dual-row DNA+AA inline translation view
description:
# Task: Dual-row DNA+AA inline translation view

## Problem
Currently users must toggle between DNA and AA view modes. For codon-level analysis, seeing both simultaneously is essential—DNA sequence with its translation aligned below.

## Solution
Implement a dual-row rendering mode in CanvasSequenceGridRenderer that shows:

```
Position: 1    4    7    10   13   16   19...
DNA:      ATG  GAC  TTA  GCC  AAA  TGT  CAG...
AA:        M    D    L    A    K    C    Q ...
```

## Technical Design

### Layout Structure
- Row 1 (top): DNA triplets with codon grouping visual cues
- Row 2 (bottom): Single AA centered under each codon
- Visual separator line between rows
- Codon boundary markers (subtle vertical lines every 3bp)

### State Management
```typescript
// Add to store
viewMode: dna | aa | dual  // Add dual option

// Add to SequenceGridOptions
dualRowMode?: boolean;
codonGrouping?: boolean;  // Show visual codon boundaries
```

### Rendering Logic
```typescript
// In CanvasSequenceGridRenderer
private renderDualRow(ctx, range, layout) {
  const codonStart = Math.floor(range.startIndex / 3) * 3;
  
  for (let i = codonStart; i < range.endIndex; i += 3) {
    // Render DNA row (3 nucleotides)
    this.renderCodon(ctx, i, rowY: 0);
    
    // Render AA row (1 amino acid centered)
    const aa = translateCodon(sequence.slice(i, i+3));
    this.renderAA(ctx, aa, i, rowY: 1);
  }
}
```

## Files to Modify

- `/packages/web/src/rendering/CanvasSequenceGridRenderer.ts` - Add dual-row render path
- `/packages/state/src/store.ts` - Add dual view mode
- `/packages/web/src/components/SequenceView.tsx` - Add UI toggle for dual mode
- `/packages/web/src/hooks/useSequenceGrid.ts` - Support dual mode

## Cell Sizing for Dual Mode

| Zoom Level | DNA Cell | AA Cell | Total Row Height |
|------------|----------|---------|------------------|
| Codon (1.0x) | 8×10px | 24×12px | 24px |
| Base (2.0x) | 16×16px | 48×18px | 36px |
| Ultra (4.0x) | 32×24px | 96×28px | 56px |

## Visual Design

- DNA row: Standard nucleotide colors
- AA row: Property-based coloring (hydrophobic=yellow, polar=green, charged=blue/red)
- Codon boundaries: Subtle 1px line every 3bp
- Reading frame indicator: Highlight current frame offset

## Dependencies

- Core translateCodon function (exists in @phage-explorer/core)
- GlyphAtlas (for AA rendering)
- Store update for new view mode

UX: Replace × character with IconX SVG in overlay close buttons
description:
## Problem

The Overlay component uses a text character × (multiplication sign or letter x) for close buttons instead of our IconX SVG component. This causes:

1. **Inconsistent rendering** - Different fonts render × differently across browsers
2. **Accessibility concerns** - Screen readers may announce it as 'multiplication' or 'times'
3. **Visual inconsistency** - Doesn't match our icon system's stroke weight/style
4. **Scaling issues** - Text characters don't scale as cleanly as SVGs

Confirmed via Playwright screenshots of Settings overlay and other modals.

## Solution

Replace the × character with IconX SVG component:

```tsx
import { IconX } from '../ui';

<button onClick={handleClose} aria-label='Close overlay'>
  <IconX size={20} />
</button>
```

## Files

- packages/web/src/components/overlays/Overlay.tsx
- packages/web/src/components/ui/icons.tsx (verify IconX exists)

## Acceptance Criteria

- Close button uses IconX SVG
- Renders consistently across Chrome, Firefox, Safari
- aria-label preserved

title: Pillar 3: Foundational Knowledge Modules
description:
## Core Educational Lessons

### What This Creates
Five standalone educational modules that can be accessed from a 'Learn' menu or linked from context help.

### Module 1: What Is a Bacteriophage?
**Content:**
- Phages as bacterial viruses (most abundant biological entities on Earth)
- Basic structure: head (capsid), tail, tail fibers
- Size context (nanometers, smaller than bacteria)
- Historical significance (Hershey-Chase, genetic code discovery)
- Modern relevance (phage therapy, biotechnology tools)

**Visuals:**
- Annotated phage diagram (T4-like, filamentous, tailless)
- Size comparison (phage vs bacteria vs human cell)
- Electron microscopy gallery

### Module 2: DNA Basics for Engineers
**Content:**
- DNA as information storage (compare to binary/text encoding)
- Four bases (A, T, G, C) as alphabet
- Double helix structure and base pairing rules
- Directionality (5' to 3') - like reading direction
- Complementary strands

**Visuals:**
- Animated base pairing (A-T, G-C)
- Interactive double helix (rotate, zoom)
- ASCII art comparison (ATGC vs 01)

### Module 3: The Central Dogma
**Content:**
- DNA → RNA → Protein pipeline
- Transcription (DNA to mRNA)
- Translation (mRNA to protein)
- Why this matters (sequence predicts function)
- Phage context (minimal genomes, overlapping genes)

**Visuals:**
- Animated flow diagram
- Ribosome 'reading' mRNA
- Before/after: sequence vs protein

### Module 4: The Genetic Code
**Content:**
- Codons as 3-letter words (64 combinations, 20 amino acids)
- Degeneracy (multiple codons → same amino acid)
- Start/stop codons
- Reading frames (shift by 1 → completely different protein)
- Why codon bias matters

**Visuals:**
- Interactive codon wheel/table
- Reading frame shifter demo
- Amino acid property wheel

### Module 5: Phage Lifecycle
**Content:**
- Lytic cycle (attach → inject → replicate → lyse)
- Lysogenic cycle (integrate → dormant → trigger)
- Temperate vs virulent phages
- Why this affects analysis (prophages in bacterial genomes)

**Visuals:**
- Animated infection cycle
- Lambda decision circuit simplified
- Prophage integration diagram

### Technical Implementation
- Each module as separate component with internal navigation
- Progress tracking (which modules completed)
- Cross-links to glossary terms
- 'Try it' sections linking to actual app features

### Files to Create
- packages/web/src/education/modules/WhatIsPhage.tsx
- packages/web/src/education/modules/DNABasics.tsx

Advanced: Periodicity & Tandem Repeat Wavelet Spectrogram
description: Detect tandem repeats, packaging motifs, and promoter periodicities via wavelets/FFT. CWT in Rust+WASM with peak picking for dominant periods/phases. Braille spectrogram under sequence grid with cursor showing period/phase. Finds periodic signals missed by motifs; links to packaging/regulation. Novelty: High, Pedagogical: High (spectral analysis, signal processing).
notes:
## PERIODICITY & TANDEM REPEAT WAVELET SPECTROGRAM

**Full Implementation from Roadmap**

### Mathematical Foundations

**Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT):**
```
W_f(a,b) = (1/√a) ∫ f(x) · ψ*((x-b)/a) dx

where:
- f(x): DNA signal (A=0, C=1, G=2, T=3 or purine/pyrimidine encoding)
- ψ: Mother wavelet (Morlet: ψ(x) = e^(iω₀x) · e^(-x²/2))
- a: Scale (inversely related to frequency/period)
- b: Position (translation)
```

**Scale-to-Period Conversion (Morlet):**
```
Period(a) = (4π × a) / (ω₀ + √(2 + ω₀²))
Typical scales: a ∈ [2, 256] for periods 2-256 bp
```

**Power Spectrogram & Peak Detection:**
```
P(a,b) = |W_f(a,b)|²
isPeak(a,b) = P(a,b) > P(a±1, b±1) AND P(a,b) > threshold × median(P)
```

**Tandem Repeat Detection via Autocorrelation:**
```
R(τ) = Σᵢ f(i) · f(i+τ)
TR_period = argmax_τ R(τ) for τ ∈ [2, 100]
```

### Complete TypeScript Implementation

- `WaveletSpectrum` interface (scales, periods, positions, power matrix, peaks)
- `SpectralPeak` with position, period, power, phase, annotation
- `TandemRepeat` with start, end, period, copies, consensus unit, purity
- `encodeDNA()` with numeric/purine/amino encodings
- `morletWavelet()` complex wavelet function
- `cwtPoint()` single point computation with Gaussian support
- `computeCWT()` full spectrogram generation
- `scaleToPeriod()` conversion function
- `findSpectralPeaks()` with local maxima and significance threshold
- `detectTandemRepeats()` autocorrelation-based detection
- `mergeOverlapping()` for tandem repeat consolidation
- `analyzePeriodicty()` full analysis pipeline
- `annotatePeriod()` biological interpretation (codon, helix, promoter)
- `renderSpectrogramASCII()` braille block visualization

### Biological Periodicities Detected

| Period | Interpretation |
|--------|----------------|
| 3 bp | Codon periodicity (coding regions) |
| 10-11 bp | DNA helical pitch (packaging signals) |
| 35-45 bp | Promoter spacing (σ factor architecture) |
| 2-6 bp | Short tandem repeats |
| 7-20 bp | Microsatellites |
| 21-100 bp | Minisatellites |

### TUI Features
- Braille spectrogram strip (period vs position)
- Scrolling synchronized with main sequence view
- Dominant periodicities table with strength bars
- Tandem repeats list with position, period, copies, consensus
- Cursor shows period and phase at current position
- [←/→] Move cursor, [P] Jump to peak, [T] Jump to repeat

### Implementation Stack
- Rust+WASM for CWT (realfft crate) for large genomes
- TS FFT fallback (fft.js) for small genomes
- SQLite cache for spectrogram tiles
- Braille block character rendering (⠀⠁⠂⠃⠄⠅⠆⠇⡀⡁...)

Novelty: 9/10, Pedagogical: 9/10, Wow Factor: 9/10

title: The rch hook blocks the wasm-compute build with exit 103 and no documented escape
description:
## The symptom

Running the documented build for the WASM package fails:

    cd packages/wasm-compute && bun run build
    ...
    Caused by: failed to execute `cargo build`: exited with exit status: 103

Exit 103 is rch's fail-closed code: "remote required; refusing local fallback".
wasm-pack shells out to `cargo build`, the rch ClaudeCode hook intercepts it, and
the fleet has no admissible worker for a wasm32 target, so it refuses rather
than building locally.

`cargo test` in the same package fails the same way:

    [RCH] remote required; refusing local fallback (all workers failed preflight
    checks) - retryable

## Why the existing opt-out does not cover it

`.rch/config.toml` already sets `[general] force_local = true` for this repo,
with a comment explaining that the suites are Bun rather than cargo and that
offloading is pure overhead here. That setting is not sufficient: the hook still
intercepts, and an inline `RCH_ENABLED=0` prefix does not bypass it either --
the rch documentation states that explicitly.

What works is exporting the wrapper bypass for the whole command:

    env RCH_CARGO_WRAPPER_BYPASS=1 RCH_ENABLED=0 bun run build
    env RCH_CARGO_WRAPPER_BYPASS=1 RCH_ENABLED=0 cargo test --release

Both were verified during phage_explorer-kalm.4 and phage_explorer-wbil.

## Why it matters

The WASM rebuild is now a required step in several workflows: the toolchain pin
(phage_explorer-kalm.4) means artifacts must be rebuilt when the pin changes,
and phage_explorer-wbil required a rebuild to ship a kernel fix. A developer or
agent following `packages/wasm-compute/package.json`'s documented `build` script
hits exit 103 with a message about workers, which points at the fleet rather
than at the local escape hatch, and nothing in this repo tells them otherwise.

This cost real time twice in one session.

## The fix

Cheapest honest version: bake the bypass into the package's own build and test
scripts, so the documented command works:

    "build": "RCH_CARGO_WRAPPER_BYPASS=1 wasm-pack build ... && ..."
    "wasm:test": "cd packages/wasm-compute && RCH_CARGO_WRAPPER_BYPASS=1 cargo test --release"

and add a line to the wasm-compute README or AGENTS.md naming exit 103 and the
variable, so the next person recognises it immediately.

Better version if the fleet is meant to build this: give a worker the wasm32
target and the pinned toolchain, then leave the hook alone. Note that this
conflicts with the recorded reasoning in `.rch/config.toml`, which concluded
offloading is overhead for this repo -- so if that changes, update that comment
too rather than leaving two rationales in the tree.

## Acceptance criteria

- `cd packages/wasm-compute && bun run build` succeeds on a machine with the rch
  hook installed, with no extra environment set by the caller.
- `bun run wasm:test` likewise.
- Exit 103 and the bypass variable are named somewhere a reader will find them.
close_reason: The documented commands work unaided. RCH_CARGO_WRAPPER_BYPASS=1 is baked into packages/wasm-compute's build and test scripts and into the root wasm:test, because wasm-pack shells out to cargo and an inline RCH_ENABLED=0 does not bypass the hook. Verified: 'cd packages/wasm-compute && bun run build' exits 0 with zero rch refusals in its output, and 'bun run wasm:test' runs all 36 Rust tests, both with no environment set by the caller. AGENTS.md gains a section naming exit 103, explaining that it is the rch hook rather than a broken toolchain, and recording that force_local in .rch/config.toml is not sufficient on its own -- which is the part that cost time twice, because the error text points at the fleet rather than at the local escape hatch. Took the cheaper of the two options in the bead: giving a worker the wasm32 target would contradict the recorded reasoning in .rch/config.toml that offloading is pure overhead for this repo.

description:
## Overview

Implement all 31 analysis overlay types that exist in the TUI, transforming ASCII visualizations into rich Canvas/WebGL graphics.

## Why This Phase Matters

Analysis overlays are the **core value proposition** of Phage Explorer. They transform raw sequence data into biological insights through:
- Statistical analysis (GC skew, complexity, k-mer anomalies)
- Structural predictions (bendability, promoters, non-B DNA)
- Evolutionary signals (HGT, selection pressure, codon bias)
- Visual patterns (dot plots, CGR, Hilbert curves)

Without these, the app is just a sequence viewer.

## Current State

### Tier 1: Already Started (8 overlays)
These exist in web but may need completion/enhancement:
- ✅ GCSkewOverlay - GC skew across genome
- ✅ ComplexityOverlay - Entropy/complexity analysis
- ✅ BendabilityOverlay - DNA bendability profile
- ✅ PromoterOverlay - Promoter site predictions
- ✅ RepeatsOverlay - Repeat finder visualization
- ✅ KmerAnomalyOverlay - K-mer anomaly heatmap
- ✅ ModuleOverlay - Functional module mapping
- ✅ TranscriptionFlowOverlay - Expression program flow

### Tier 2: Missing (17 overlays)
These need to be created from scratch:
- PackagingPressureOverlay - DNA packaging constraints
- VirionStabilityOverlay - Virion structural stability
- PhasePortraitOverlay - AA property PCA scatter
- BiasDecompositionOverlay - Codon bias PCA
- HGTOverlay - Horizontal gene transfer islands
- CRISPROverlay - CRISPR spacer mapping
- SyntenyOverlay - Gene order conservation
- TropismOverlay - Host receptor predictions
- StructureConstraintOverlay - RNA structure constraints
- NonBDNAOverlay - G-quadruplex, Z-DNA, cruciform
- AnomalyOverlay - Statistical anomaly detection
- DotPlotOverlay - Self-similarity matrix
- CGROverlay - Chaos Game Representation
- HilbertOverlay - Hilbert curve visualization
- GelOverlay - Virtual gel electrophoresis

### Supporting Components (3 additional)
- AAKeyOverlay - Amino acid color reference
- AALegend - Compact AA legend
- SearchOverlay - Phage search interface

## Architecture Pattern

All overlays follow a consistent pattern:

```typescript
export function [Name]Overlay() {
  // 1. Get sequence from store
  const sequence = usePhageStore(s => s.currentPhage?.sequence ?? '');
  
  // 2. Get or compute analysis data (via worker)
  const data = useAnalysisResult('[name]', sequence);
  
  // 3. Render with standard overlay wrapper
  return (
    <Overlay title="[Name] Analysis" onClose={...}>
      <AnalysisCanvas data={data} />
      <StatisticsPanel data={data} />
    </Overlay>
  );
}
```

## Visualization Upgrades (ASCII → Canvas)

| TUI ASCII | Web Canvas | Enhancement |
|-----------|-----------|-------------|
| Text sparklines | Sparkline.tsx | Smooth curves, hover values |
| ASCII heatmaps | HeatmapCanvas | Color gradients, zoom |
| Text scatter plots | ScatterCanvas | Interactive PCA exploration |
| Box-drawing charts | SVG/Canvas | Animation, interactivity |
| ASCII dot matrix | Canvas ImageData | Full resolution |

## Dependencies

- **Depends on**: Phase 1 (database), Phase 2 (core views for context)
- **Blocks**: None directly, but needed for feature parity

## Success Criteria

- [ ] All 8 Tier 1 overlays fully functional
- [ ] All 17 Tier 2 overlays implemented
- [ ] Each overlay has Canvas-based visualization
- [ ] Analysis runs in Web Worker (non-blocking)
- [ ] Loading states while computing
- [ ] Can trigger overlays via keyboard shortcuts
- [ ] Menu system lists all available overlays

title: PhasePortraitOverlay - Amino acid property PCA scatter plot
description:
Implement overlay for visualizing amino acid usage patterns through PCA-based phase portrait analysis.

## Biological Significance
Amino acid usage reflects:
- Codon optimization strategies
- tRNA availability in host
- Protein structural preferences
- Evolutionary adaptation signatures
- Horizontal gene transfer events (HGT clusters separately)

Phase portraits reveal global proteome organization and identify genes with unusual compositional properties that may indicate recent HGT or specialized functions.

## Visualization Type
Interactive 2D scatter plot (PCA phase space):
- Each point = one ORF/protein
- X-axis: PC1 (primary variation, typically hydrophobicity)
- Y-axis: PC2 (secondary variation, often charge/size)
- Color coding by: functional category, GC%, or expression level
- Interactive selection and zoom
- Outlier highlighting

## Worker Integration
Create `workers/phase-portrait-worker.ts`:
- Extract amino acid composition for each ORF (20-dimensional vectors)
- Compute PCA transformation (reduce to 2-3 dimensions)
- Calculate loadings to interpret PC axes
- Identify outliers using Mahalanobis distance
- Cluster genes by AA usage patterns
- Correlate with other features (GC%, position, function)

## Implementation Details

### Files to Create
1. `src/tui/overlays/PhasePortraitOverlay.tsx`
   - Interactive scatter plot using ScatterCanvas primitive
   - Point selection and highlighting
   - Axis labels with PC variance explained
   - Loading vectors display (which AAs drive each PC)
   - Outlier annotations

2. `src/workers/phase-portrait-worker.ts`
   - AA composition calculation
   - PCA implementation (eigen decomposition)
   - Outlier detection algorithms
   - Clustering (k-means or DBSCAN)
   - Feature correlation analysis

### Dependencies
- **Requires**: Visualization primitives task (ScatterCanvas.tsx)
- Set dependency after primitives task is created

### Keyboard Shortcut
- **Alt+Shift+P** - Toggle phase portrait overlay

### Data Flow
1. User activates overlay (Alt+Shift+P)
2. Worker receives all ORF sequences
3. Worker computes:
   - 20-dimensional AA frequency vectors for each ORF
   - PCA transformation matrix
   - PC scores for all ORFs
   - Variance explained by each PC
   - Loading vectors (AA contributions)
4. Worker identifies outliers (>3σ from centroid)
5. UI renders scatter plot with interactive features
6. User can:
   - Hover to see ORF details
   - Click to highlight ORF in main viewer
   - Toggle color schemes
   - View loading vectors

## Display Features
- **Scatter points**: ORFs positioned by PC1/PC2 scores
- **Color schemes**: 
  - Functional category (structural, replication, lysis, etc.)
  - GC% gradient
  - Expression level (if predicted)
  - Outlier status
- **Loadings biplot**: Arrows showing AA contributions to PCs
- **Variance info**: "PC1: 45.2% variance, PC2: 23.1% variance"
- **Outlier labels**: Annotate unusual genes

## Biological Interpretation Guide
- **PC1 typically represents**: Hydrophobicity vs hydrophilicity
- **PC2 typically represents**: Charge or size patterns
- **Tight cluster**: Core conserved genes with host-adapted codon usage
- **Outliers**: Potential HGT, recent acquisition, or specialized function

## Testing Considerations

title: StructureConstraintOverlay - RNA structure constraints
description:
Implement overlay for predicting and visualizing RNA secondary structure constraints that affect genome organization and expression.

## Biological Significance
RNA structures in phage genomes serve critical roles:
- Ribosome binding sites (RBS) for translation initiation
- Transcription terminators (rho-independent)
- Riboswitches and regulatory elements
- Packaging signals (pac sites)
- Anti-sense regulation between overlapping genes

This overlay reveals hidden functional RNA elements through thermodynamic folding predictions.

## Visualization Type
Multi-layer visualization:
- **Structure heatmap**: Base-pairing probability matrix (triangular)
- **Energy landscape**: Minimum free energy (MFE) profile across genome
- **Secondary structure diagrams**: Arc plots for high-confidence structures
- **Functional element annotations**: RBS, terminators, riboswitches
- **Conservation track**: Structure conservation in related phages

## Worker Integration
Create `workers/structure-worker.ts`:
- RNA secondary structure prediction (Vienna RNAfold algorithm)
- Base-pairing probability calculations
- Minimum free energy (MFE) sliding windows
- RBS detection (Shine-Dalgarno sequences)
- Terminator prediction (stem-loop + poly-U)
- Riboswitch motif scanning
- Structure conservation analysis

## Implementation Details

### Files to Create
1. `src/tui/overlays/StructureConstraintOverlay.tsx`
   - Triangular heatmap for pairing probabilities (HeatmapCanvas)
   - Arc diagram for secondary structures (ArcDiagram)
   - Energy profile plot
   - Functional element track
   - Interactive structure browser

2. `src/workers/structure-worker.ts`
   - RNA folding algorithms (implement simplified Vienna/Nussinov)
   - Energy parameter tables (Turner 2004 model)
   - RBS detection (sequence motifs + spacing)
   - Terminator prediction (stem-loop energy + U-tract)
   - Riboswitch HMMs (Rfam database)

### Dependencies
- **Requires**: Visualization primitives task (HeatmapCanvas, ArcDiagram)

### Keyboard Shortcut
- **Alt+R** - Toggle structure constraint overlay

### Data Flow
1. User activates overlay (Alt+R)
2. Worker receives genome sequence (DNA → transcribed to RNA)
3. Worker performs sliding window analysis (200-500 nt windows):
   - Predict secondary structure (MFE and suboptimal)
   - Calculate base-pairing probabilities
   - Compute ensemble free energies
4. Worker detects functional elements:
   - Scan for RBS upstream of ORFs (16S rRNA complementarity)
   - Identify terminators downstream of genes
   - Search for riboswitch motifs
5. Worker generates pairing probability matrix
6. UI renders multi-layer visualization
7. User can:
   - Zoom into regions
   - Click structure to see details
   - Toggle functional element highlights

## Display Layers

### 1. Base-Pairing Probability Heatmap
- Triangular matrix (position i vs position j)
- Color intensity = pairing probability (0-1)
- Strong pairs (>0.9) = dark blue
- Weak pairs (<0.3) = light blue/white

### 2. MFE Energy Profile
- Line graph showing ΔG per window
- More negative = more stable structures
- Peaks indicate unstable regions (regulatory?)

### 3. Secondary Structure Arcs
- Arc diagram connecting paired bases
- Arc height = pairing distance
- Color by pairing type (GC, AU, GU wobble)
- Only show high-confidence pairs (>0.8)

### 4. Functional Element Track
- **RBS**: Green boxes upstream of ORFs
- **Terminators**: Red stem-loop symbols
- **Riboswitches**: Purple boxes with motif name
- **Packaging signals**: Orange markers

### 5. Conservation Track (if multi-genome)
- Compare structure conservation vs sequence conservation
- Compensatory mutations indicate functional structures

## RNA Folding Algorithm
Use dynamic programming approach (Nussinov or simplified Vienna):
1. Initialize DP matrix for base-pairing
2. Apply thermodynamic parameters (stacking, loops, bulges)
3. Trace back to find MFE structure
4. Calculate partition function for probabilities
5. Identify suboptimal structures within 10% of MFE

## Functional Element Detection

### RBS (Ribosome Binding Site)
- Scan -20 to -5 nt upstream of start codons
- Look for Shine-Dalgarno: AGGAGG (allow 1 mismatch)
- Calculate spacing to AUG (optimal 5-9 nt)
- Check for secondary structure occlusion

### Terminators
- Scan downstream of stop codons
- Detect stem-loop (ΔG < -10 kcal/mol)
- Check for poly-U tract (≥4 U's after stem)
- Intrinsic (rho-independent) vs rho-dependent

### Riboswitches
- Scan with Rfam covariance models
- Common in prophages: TPP, FMN, SAM riboswitches
- Detect conserved structure + sequence motifs

## Performance Optimization
- Pre-compute energy tables
- Use sparse matrix for pairing probabilities
- Limit window size for long genomes (>100 kb)
- Web Worker offloading for heavy calculations

## Scientific References
- Zuker & Stiegler (1981) RNA folding algorithm
- Turner et al. (2004) Thermodynamic parameters
- Rfam database for riboswitch motifs
- Stormo et al. (1982) RBS prediction

## Testing Considerations
- Validate RBS predictions with experimental data
- Compare terminator predictions with RNA-seq data
- Check structure predictions against crystallographic data (if available)
- Test performance with large genomes (T4 ~170 kb)

title: NonBDNAOverlay - G-quadruplex, Z-DNA, cruciform structures
description:
Implement overlay for detecting and visualizing non-B-form DNA structures including G-quadruplexes, Z-DNA, and cruciform structures in phage genomes.

## Biological Significance
Non-B-DNA structures have important biological roles:
- **G-quadruplexes (G4)**: Regulatory elements, affect transcription/replication
- **Z-DNA**: Left-handed helix, forms in high-GC regions under torsional stress
- **Cruciforms**: Hairpin structures at inverted repeats, recombination hotspots
- **Triplexes**: H-DNA formation, gene regulation
- **A-DNA**: Dehydrated form, packaging-related

These structures can affect:
- Gene expression and regulation
- DNA packaging and ejection
- Recombination and genome rearrangement
- Evolutionary hotspots

## Visualization Type
Multi-track linear genome view:
- **G4 track**: Predicted G-quadruplex forming sequences
- **Z-DNA track**: High Z-DNA propensity regions
- **Cruciform track**: Inverted repeat regions
- **Triplex track**: Potential H-DNA sites
- **Structure stability**: ΔG or propensity scores
- **Feature details panel**: Structure parameters and scores

## Worker Integration
Create `workers/nonbdna-worker.ts`:
- G-quadruplex prediction (regex + folding energy)
- Z-DNA propensity calculation (dinucleotide scores)
- Inverted repeat detection for cruciforms
- Triplex-forming oligonucleotide (TFO) prediction
- Structure stability scoring
- Overlap analysis with functional elements

   - Multi-track genome visualization (GenomeTrack)
